content: Antiviral drugs are a specific category of medications designed to treat viral infections. Similar to antibiotics, which target bacteria, antiviral drugs are tailored to combat specific viruses. These drugs belong to a broader group of antimicrobials, which also includes antifungal, antiparasitic, and antibacterial agents. Antiviral drugs are generally safe for the host organism and are used to manage infections without causing significant harm. It is important to distinguish antiviral drugs from viricides, which deactivate virus particles outside the body. Currently, most antiviral drugs are developed to address infections caused by HIV, herpesviruses (which are responsible for conditions like cold sores and other diseases), and hepatitis B and C viruses, which can lead to liver cancer. Researchers are actively working to expand the range of antiviral drugs to target other viral families. The development of antiviral drugs has been driven by advancements in understanding the genetic and molecular mechanisms of viruses, improvements in drug discovery techniques, and the urgent need to address the HIV/AIDS pandemic. However, like other antimicrobial agents, antiviral drugs face the challenge of drug resistance, as viruses evolve mechanisms to survive treatment. As of 2007, smallpox is the only viral disease that has been successfully eradicated, with polio eradication efforts still ongoing. Both of these efforts rely on vaccines. History of Antiviral Development Modern medicine has developed numerous tools, such as antiseptics, vaccines, and antibiotics, to combat infections. However, historically, medicine has struggled to develop effective treatments for viral infections. While vaccines have been successful in preventing certain viral diseases, there was little that could be done for individuals already infected with a virus, apart from recommending rest and hydration. The first experimental antiviral drugs were developed in the 1960s, primarily targeting herpesviruses. These early drugs were discovered using traditional trial-and-error methods. Researchers grew cultures of cells infected with the target virus, introduced various chemicals, and observed whether viral activity increased or decreased. Promising chemicals were then studied further. This process was time-consuming and inefficient, especially without a detailed understanding of how the target virus functioned. Significant progress was made in the 1980s when researchers began unraveling the full genetic sequences of viruses. This allowed for a deeper understanding of viral mechanisms and the identification of specific chemical targets to disrupt their reproductive cycles. Since then, dozens of antiviral treatments have been developed, and ongoing research continues to leverage new knowledge and technologies to create more effective drugs. The Viral Life Cycle Viruses consist of a genome (DNA or RNA) and, in some cases, a few enzymes encased in a protein capsule. Some viruses also have a lipid envelope. Unlike living organisms, viruses cannot reproduce independently. Instead, they hijack a host cell's machinery to replicate themselves, producing the next generation of viruses. Researchers developing antiviral drugs aim to disrupt the viral life cycle at various stages. While the details of viral life cycles vary by species, they generally follow a common pattern: 1. Attachment to a host cell. 2. Release of viral genetic material and enzymes into the host cell. 3. Replication of viral components using the host cell's machinery. 4. Assembly of viral components into complete viral particles. 5. Release of new viral particles to infect additional host cells. Limitations of Vaccines Vaccines are designed to target viruses in their complete particle stage, outside of host cells. Traditional vaccines consist of weakened or inactivated versions of a pathogen, while newer subunit vaccines use specific protein targets from the pathogen. Vaccines stimulate the immune system to recognize and respond to the pathogen without causing significant harm to the host. When the actual pathogen attacks, the immune system can respond quickly and block the infection. Vaccines are highly effective against stable viruses but are less useful for treating individuals who are already infected. They are also less effective against rapidly mutating viruses, such as influenza (which requires annual vaccine updates) and HIV. These limitations highlight the need for antiviral drugs. Antiviral Targeting Techniques Modern antiviral drug design focuses on identifying viral proteins or protein components that can be disabled. These targets are chosen to minimize side effects by ensuring they are as distinct as possible from human proteins. Ideally, the targets should also be conserved across multiple strains of a virus or even across different species within the same viral family, allowing a single drug to have broad effectiveness. For example, researchers may target a critical enzyme synthesized by the virus but not by the host. Once targets are identified, candidate drugs can be selected from existing compounds or designed at the molecular level using computer-aided tools. The target proteins can be produced in the laboratory for testing with candidate treatments using rapid screening technologies. Approaches by Life Cycle Stage Before Cell Entry One strategy is to prevent the virus from entering the host cell. This involves blocking the virus's ability to bind to specific receptor molecules on the host cell's surface or preventing the virus from uncoating and releasing its contents inside the cell. For viruses with a lipid envelope, this also involves inhibiting the fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane. Drugs can achieve this by mimicking viral proteins (VAPs) to bind to cellular receptors or by mimicking receptors to bind to VAPs. Examples include entry-blocking drugs like amantadine and rimantadine for influenza, and pleconaril, which targets rhinoviruses (responsible for the common cold) by blocking a pocket on the virus's surface that controls uncoating. During Viral Synthesis Another approach targets the processes that synthesize viral components after the virus has invaded a cell. Nucleotide or nucleoside analogues, which resemble the building blocks of RNA or DNA, can deactivate the enzymes responsible for viral genome synthesis. Acyclovir, the first successful antiviral drug, is a nucleoside analogue effective against herpesvirus infections. Zidovudine (AZT), the first antiviral approved for HIV treatment, is also a nucleoside analogue. Improved understanding of reverse transcriptase, an enzyme used by HIV and hepatitis B for replication, has led to the development of better nucleoside analogues and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. Other targets for HIV antivirals include RNase H (a component of reverse transcriptase) and integrase (which incorporates viral DNA into the host genome). Antisense molecules, designed as mirror images of critical viral genome sections, can bind to and block the operation of those genomes. Fomivirsen, an antisense drug, is used to treat cytomegalovirus-related eye infections in AIDS patients. Ribozymes, synthetic enzymes that cut viral RNA or DNA at specific sites, are also being developed to target viruses like hepatitis C and HIV. Release Phase The final stage of the viral life cycle involves the release of completed viruses from the host cell. Drugs like zanamivir (Relenza) and oseltamivir (Tamiflu) target influenza by blocking neuraminidase, a molecule on the surface of flu viruses that facilitates their release. These drugs are effective across a wide range of flu strains. Immune System Stimulation Some antiviral strategies focus on stimulating the body's immune system to attack viruses rather than directly targeting the viruses themselves. Interferons, which inhibit viral synthesis in infected cells, are a well-known example. Interferon alpha is used to treat hepatitis B and C, and other interferons are being investigated for various diseases. Another approach involves synthesizing monoclonal antibodies, which bind to specific targets on pathogens and mark them for attack by the immune system. Monoclonal drugs are being developed to combat respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants and hepatitis B. Some viruses produce proteins that mimic human immune system proteins, confusing the immune response. Researchers are working to develop antivirals that can recognize and disable these mimic proteins.
